candidate.title: MIPSTR
candidate.scope: MIPSTR as depicted in the middle row of the supplied Illumina DNA Low-Level Detection schematic, interpreted using the Carlson et al. MIPSTR primary paper (Genome Research 2015; DOI 10.1101/gr.182212.114). The target is tagged smMIP capture and sequencing of genomic STR loci, with between-individual and within-individual variation readouts. The upper smMIP and lower MDA/IMS-MDA/MIDAS rows are separate neighboring catalogue workflows, not alternatives of the assigned MIPSTR card. Within MIPSTR, smMIP capture is a component, not a second target method. This record describes the drawn architecture rather than every library-construction or computational step of the primary implementation.

states.label: Genomic DNA containing targeted STR loci
features: Biological target: repeat-unit variation at selected genomic STR loci, with flanking DNA providing locus identity.
Per-individual or per-strain sample identity must be retained to interpret the two readout cartoons; no single-cell compartment or cell barcode is drawn.
Yellow-highlighted STR on a blue genomic line is an illustrative target, not a chemical modification.

evidence.quote: We used single-molecule Molecular Inversion Probes (smMIPs) (Hiatt et al. 2013) to capture STRs, thereby maximizing the number of STR-spanning, informative reads.

states.label: STR-targeting single-molecule molecular inversion probes
features: Oligonucleotide probes contain two STR-flanking targeting arms, a common backbone for PCR/sequencing priming, and a degenerate molecular tag.
The primary MIPSTR implementation uses a 12-nt degenerate tag that identifies a capture event; it is not the sample index and does not identify a cell.

evidence.quote: For each targeted STR, we designed a MIP, which is an 80-nt oligonucleotide that contains (1) targeting arms which will uniquely hybridize to STR flanking regions; (2) a 12-nt degenerate tag to distinguish individual capture events; and (3) a common backbone for PCR and sequencing priming (Fig. 1A; Hiatt et al. 2013).

states.label: Gapped smMIP–genomic STR hybridization complexes
features: Probe arms hybridize on opposite sides of an STR-containing target region, leaving that region to be copied.
The probe backbone loops above the genomic template; the red segment is labeled Degenerate molecular tag.
The tag is already part of the probe before copying and amplification.

states.label: STR-copy-containing circularized probes shown against their genomic templates
features: Polymerase extension copies the target STR and flanking gap into the probe, and ligation closes the probe circle.
The closed probe carries the copied target together with its pre-existing degenerate tag and common backbone.
The drawing retains the genomic line below the copied probe; this boundary is not a claim of purified circles or of sequencing the original genomic DNA.

states.label: Amplified MIPSTR sequencing library
features: PCR products derive from the captured, circularized probe products and carry the copied STR with probe sequences needed to recover locus and capture-event identity.
In the primary implementation an indexed reverse PCR primer supplies sample identity; this is a separate association from the degenerate molecular tag.
This is a targeted probe-copy library, not a whole-genome library and not a library of intact cells.

evidence.locator: MIPSTR row: arrow following Copy target STR, labeled Amplify and sequence

evidence.quote: To create sequencing libraries, we amplified the capture reactions using a common forward primer and an indexed reverse primer.

For each targeted STR, we designed a MIP, which is an 80-nt oligonucleotide that contains (1) targeting arms which will uniquely hybridize to STR flanking regions; (2) a 12-nt degenerate tag to distinguish individual capture events; and (3) a common backbone for PCR and sequencing priming (Fig. 1A; Hiatt et al. 2013).

We sorted reads according to their MIP targeting arms, and for each MIP, used BWA (Li and Durbin 2009) to map its corresponding reads to a set of synthetic reference sequences designed specifically for each targeted STR (Fig. 1D).

states.label: MIPSTR reads retaining sample, STR locus, and capture-event associations
features: The primary implementation reads the STR target and ligation arm in the forward read, the degenerate tag and extension arm in the paired reverse read, and sample identity in an index read.
Sample barcode, targeting-arm sequence, and molecular tag associate a read with an individual, a locus, and a capture event, respectively.
Amplification can create STR stutter, so raw read counts or raw repeat-length differences do not by themselves identify independent biological alleles.
The schematic depicts amplification and sequencing as one broad block; the forward/reverse/index interfaces are paper-supported clarifications rather than additional drawn steps.

evidence.locator: MIPSTR row: arrow following Copy target STR, labeled Amplify and sequence

evidence.quote: We collected one 250-bp forward read to determine sequence of the ligation arm and STR target locus, one 50-bp reverse read to determine the sequence of the degenerate tag and extension arm, and one 8-bp read to determine the sample index sequence.

For these pooled libraries, we sorted reads first by strain-specific barcode, then by targeting arm to identify the STR locus and degenerate MIP tag to identify reads originating from the same capture event (Fig. 1B,C).

For each tag-defined read group (i.e., reads containing the same MIP tag), we assumed that the mode of called unit numbers across reads is the true allele for this capture event (Fig. 3). STR unit number variation within a tag-defined read group is considered technical error (Fig. 3; Supplemental Table 1).

states.label: STR genotypes and natural variation between individuals
features: Readout compares STR unit-number alleles at the same targeted loci across identified individuals; the cartoon labels the compared samples Strain I and Strain II.
The different loop lengths summarize repeat-length variation, not a transfer or pooling of the illustrated strains.
Interpretation is limited to captured, informative loci; variable capture performance and extreme expansions can leave loci inaccessible.

evidence.locator: MIPSTR row, first readout cartoon: Strain I and Strain II above Natural variation between individuals

evidence.quote: (B) Capture across genetically diverse individuals identifies germline STR variation across genetically diverse individuals. (C) MIPSTR distinguishes somatic STR variation from technical error, using many degenerate tags. STR variation within a tag-defined read group (i.e., reads with the same degenerate tag) is considered technical error. STR variation across tag-defined read groups is considered somatic variation.
These extreme expansions are not directly accessible with MIPSTR due to our inability to capture and sequence both flanking regions.
Another limitation of MIP-based methods is the well-known high variability in MIP performance (Porreca et al. 2007; Turner et al. 2009; Boyle et al. 2014).

evidence.locator: MIPSTR row, the two terminal Strain I/Strain II cartoons under the between-individual and within-individual captions
evidence.rationale: The different loop sizes are interpreted as illustrative STR length alleles because the row targets STRs, the captions distinguish variation between and within individuals, and primary Figure 1B/C describes those same two comparisons. These cartoons are readout illustrations, not evidence for mixing strains, transferring material between them, or assigning capture tags to cells.

states.label: Evidence for within-individual STR variation, qualified against technical error
features: Tag-defined read groups represent independent capture events at a locus; repeat-unit variation within a tag group is treated as technical error in the paper.
Differences supported across capture groups can support within-individual biological heterogeneity, including somatic STR variants.

The figure labels this endpoint Somatic variation within an individual, but between-tag variation can also reflect heterozygosity or locus duplication; the tag itself does not identify the originating cell.

evidence.locator: MIPSTR row, second readout cartoon: Strain I and Strain II above Somatic variation within an individual

evidence.quote: (B) Capture across genetically diverse individuals identifies germline STR variation across genetically diverse individuals. (C) MIPSTR distinguishes somatic STR variation from technical error, using many degenerate tags. STR variation within a tag-defined read group (i.e., reads with the same degenerate tag) is considered technical error. STR variation across tag-defined read groups is considered somatic variation.

However, unit number variation observed among different MIP molecules, each representing independent capture events, is potentially the result of heterozygosity, somatic variation, or duplication (Figs. 1C, 3).

We then sorted the STR genotype calls by the degenerate tag on the paired reverse read from which they derived. We required an exact match of the 12-bp degenerate tag for reads to be grouped into a tag-defined read group. We then called the mode STR unit number of each tag-defined read group as the genotype of that DNA molecule. If we observed that more than one tag-defined read group supported an alternate STR allele, we considered it evidence of somatic variation.

operations.label: Targeted capture of STR loci by smMIPs (MIPSTR)
operations.description: STR-flanking arms of tagged probes hybridize to genomic DNA, forming gapped target–probe complexes around STR loci. The genomic target remains the template; capture associates its locus with a tag-bearing probe before amplification.
operations.mechanism: Locus-specific hybridization of the extension and ligation arms to unique sequences flanking the STR.
operations.information_effect: Target selection is encoded by probe-arm sequence; the probe already carries the degenerate tag used later to identify a capture event.

operations.label: Copy target STR
operations.description: The hybridized probe is extended across the STR-containing gap using genomic DNA as template, and ligation produces a closed probe carrying the target copy. The drawn genomic line remains beneath the copied probe.

operations.information_effect: A DNA copy of the STR is physically joined to the probe backbone and degenerate tag, connecting repeat sequence with a preamplification capture-event identifier.

operations.label: Amplify and sequence
operations.description: Captured probe circles provide templates for amplification, yielding a targeted sequencing library and reads of the copied STR and associated probe information. The diagram combines these actions in one transition and does not separately depict cleanup, pooling, or sequencing-primer installation.
operations.mechanism: The primary implementation amplifies capture products with a common forward primer and indexed reverse primer, and obtains paired target/tag reads plus a sample-index read. Routine unshown library-construction steps are not expanded into operations.
operations.information_effect: Amplification preserves the capture tag on descendants of a captured molecule, while an independent sample index links the library to its individual. Sequencing exposes the STR and those associations; PCR may introduce repeat stutter.

operations.label: Natural variation between individuals
operations.description: Interpret reads at the same targeted STR loci across identified individuals to compare repeat-unit genotypes. This is one readout of the capture/sequencing route, illustrated by the first Strain I/Strain II cartoon.
operations.mechanism: The primary paper identifies the locus through targeting-arm sequence and assigns STR unit-number alleles using locus-specific synthetic reference sequences. operations.label: Somatic variation within an individual
operations.description: Within a sample and locus, compare repeat-unit calls within and across tag-defined read groups to distinguish amplification stutter from supported biological STR heterogeneity. This is a second interpretation of the same sequencing output; no arrow carries the first readout into this cartoon.
operations.mechanism: The primary paper uses the modal STR unit number in a tag-defined group as the captured molecule’s allele. Within-group variation is treated as technical error, while support across independent capture groups can support an alternate allele.
operations.information_effect: Supports detection of low-frequency STR variation within an individual. The cartoon’s somatic label is qualified by the paper: between-capture differences can also arise from heterozygosity or duplication, and tag grouping does not determine a variant’s cell of origin.

method_scopes.rationale: The card title and explicitly labeled MIPSTR row select this one target method. All five operations belong to this row: tagged capture, STR copying/circularization, one broad amplification/sequencing block, and two distinct readout interpretations. The adjacent upper smMIP row supplies neither a separate target nor an asserted material route into MIPSTR. Probe circularization and the target/tag/sample read interfaces are resolved by the MIPSTR primary paper. The two terminal cartoons illustrate between-individual and within-individual comparisons; their horizontal placement does not establish a serial transfer, so both consume the sequencing-data state independently. The primary A. thaliana implementation clarifies the architecture without adding specimen preparation or other unshown assays.

corrections.primary_statement: The primary MIPSTR paper compares tag-defined read groups to distinguish amplification error, but explicitly states that unit-number variation among capture events can arise from heterozygosity, somatic variation, or duplication. The authored readout therefore preserves the somatic endpoint as a supported application while withholding a universal rule that any between-tag difference is somatic.
